title: Romanticism
summary: Romanticism as the school committed to volition, and its place in Rand's esthetics.

lessons.title: Where a school sits
lessons.objective: Locate Romanticism as a school inside esthetics, named by its view of man, not by a feeling.

exercises.prompt: What does esthetics study, in the branch where this unit sits?

feedback.note: Esthetics is the study of art. Romanticism is placed inside that study, not in politics or in a lab.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what names a school of art?

choices.text: The century on the copyright page

feedback.note: A school is a fundamental view of man as art presents him. Date, palette, and biography do not name the school.

exercises.prompt: Match each name to the job this unit gives it.

pairs.right: A basic view of man in art

feedback.note: Keep the three levels apart: the branch, the kind of classification, and the school this unit teaches.

exercises.prompt: Complete the placement.

feedback.note: It sits inside esthetics as a school. It is not an extra branch beside metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and politics, and it is not a mood.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that places the school.

feedback.note: The school is an esthetic classification. Politics is a different branch.

exercises.prompt: Which name does this unit use for the school committed to volition?

feedback.note: Romanticism is the name of that commitment. Naturalism is the contrast you will meet later, not this name.

exercises.prompt: What is the second job of this unit, after naming the commitment?

choices.text: To place the school in her esthetics
To rank living painters by fame

feedback.note: The unit teaches the commitment to volition and where that school sits in her esthetics. Fame, price, and statutes are outside it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the commitment named in the unit summary.

feedback.note: Volition is the commitment. Fashion, nostalgia, and luck are not what the school is named for.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about what a school states.

feedback.note: The classification is a view of man. Weather is scenery, not the school.

lessons.title: The premise of volition
lessons.objective: State the premise that defines Romanticism: man can choose.

exercises.prompt: What premise defines Romanticism?

feedback.note: The school stands on volition: man can choose. Forces that erase choice are the opposite premise.

exercises.prompt: Under that premise, what sets a character's course?

feedback.note: Setting can matter, but the Romantic premise is that the person chooses a course rather than only undergoing one.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to what the premise says about it.

pairs.right: Possible because a choice can be wrong

feedback.note: If choice is real, a person can pick a value, pursue it, and also miss. That is the premise at work.

exercises.prompt: Complete the defining claim.

feedback.note: The faculty named here is volition. The school does not claim that man knows everything, cannot be hurt, or holds a title.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the premise.

feedback.note: Can choose is the premise. Cannot would cancel the school.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, volition means which power?

feedback.note: Volition is the faculty of choice. Intensity of feeling, muscle, and status are different facts.

exercises.prompt: A story insists the hero could not have done otherwise. What has happened to the Romantic premise?

choices.text: The premise has just been named

feedback.note: If no alternative was open, choice was not real in that story. That is a dropped premise, not a proof of it.

exercises.prompt: Name what the school will not drop.

feedback.note: Costume, dialect, and scenery can change. The premise that stays is choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to the premise it shows.

feedback.note: The test is whether choice is real. Values pursued by decision are what that reality looks like in the work.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about characters.

feedback.note: Action by choice is the premise in story form. Reflex and drift are not substitutes for it.

lessons.title: Against the denial of choice
lessons.objective: Tell Romanticism from the school that presents man as determined.

exercises.prompt: Which view is the contrast to Romanticism in this unit?

choices.text: Man is a product of forces he does not choose
Maps should be drawn to scale

feedback.note: The opposing view denies choice and treats man as determined by forces. Scale and rhyme are not the contrast.

exercises.prompt: In this contrast, what does Naturalism do with volition?

choices.text: It is the name of the volitional school
It proves that anyone can choose
It is only a rule about paintbrushes

feedback.note: Naturalism, as the contrast here, is the school that denies volition. Romanticism is the school that holds it.

exercises.prompt: Match each school to its stand on choice.

feedback.note: The split is volition versus the denial of volition. That is the whole contrast between the two schools.

exercises.prompt: Complete the contrast.

feedback.note: Denies is the relation. Naturalism is not a hymn to volition and not a brush technique.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about a determined man.

feedback.note: Determination, in this contrast, means the course is not chosen. That is why it is not Romanticism.

exercises.prompt: Heredity and the street alone decide the ending. Which premise is the story carrying?

choices.text: Both schools at once, with no difference
No view of man at all, by definition

feedback.note: If only unchosen forces decide the end, the story is not carrying the premise that man chooses.

exercises.prompt: Both schools can use realistic detail. What actually splits them?

choices.text: Whether man is shown as able to choose

feedback.note: Realistic detail can appear on either side. The school is fixed by the view of choice, not by how solid the furniture looks.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about the split.

parts.text: , not about how real the furniture looks.

feedback.note: Volition is the issue. Upholstery, page count, and ink do not classify the school.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence about what does not decide the school.

feedback.note: Detail is not the classifier. Volition is, which is why it is the distractor you leave out of this sentence.

lessons.title: Not a mood
lessons.objective: Separate Romanticism from the popular mix-up with emotion, mysticism, or escape from facts.

exercises.prompt: Does feeling strongly, by itself, make a work Romantic?

choices.text: Only if the feeling is sadness

feedback.note: Intensity is not the definition. The school is a commitment to volition, not a measure of how hard someone feels.

exercises.prompt: Is escape from the facts what Romanticism is committed to?

choices.text: No. The commitment is volition, not a cancellation of facts
Yes. The school exists to leave reality
Yes, if the setting is a dream
Yes, if the costumes are old

feedback.note: The school re-creates a world in which people choose. It does not mean flight from facts, dreams, or period costume.

exercises.prompt: Match each popular stand-in to what this unit says about it.

feedback.note: Feeling and mysticism are common mix-ups. Volition is what the school actually commits to.

exercises.prompt: Complete the correction.

feedback.note: Mood, fog, and costume can decorate any school. They do not replace the commitment to volition.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that rejects the mix-up.

feedback.note: Emotion does not define it. The distractor would reverse the point.

exercises.prompt: A gloomy mystical tale shows no chosen action. Is it Romantic just because it is intense?

feedback.note: Intensity, gloom, castles, and swelling music do not supply the premise. Without chosen action, it is not this school.

exercises.prompt: A bright adventure shows nothing chosen. Does the cheerful tone make it Romantic?

choices.text: No. Tone is not the test
Yes, if the pace is fast
Yes, if someone is called a hero

feedback.note: Cheer and gloom are both tones. The test remains whether the work treats man as able to choose.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that names the test.

feedback.note: Choice is the test. Intensity and costume are the mix-ups this lesson sets aside.

lessons.title: What the premise makes visible
lessons.objective: Connect the volitional premise to purposeful action in art, and to why the school belongs in her esthetics.

exercises.prompt: Because man can choose, what can a work show besides events that are only endured?

choices.text: Nothing but a list of objects
Nothing a person could aim at

feedback.note: Volition makes selected values visible. A list or a weather report does not use that premise.

exercises.prompt: Why does purposeful action belong to this school?

choices.text: Purpose is only a rhyme scheme
Purpose means the work is short

feedback.note: A purpose is an end someone chooses to pursue. Without a chooser, the action is not purposeful in this sense.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its role in this unit.

pairs.right: Action aimed at a chosen end
The branch where the school is placed

feedback.note: Volition is the premise, purpose is what that premise lets action be, and esthetics is where the school is classified.

exercises.prompt: Complete why the school belongs in her esthetics.

parts.text: It belongs there because she takes man to be a being of

feedback.note: Her view of man is volitional consciousness. Romanticism is the esthetic school that projects that fact, not an automatic, tribal, or merely decorative premise.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that links purpose to choice.

feedback.note: A chooser is required. A crowd count or a rhyme does not supply a purpose.

exercises.prompt: Where does Romanticism sit, and what does it not replace?

choices.text: Inside esthetics, as the school that projects volition

feedback.note: The place is inside esthetics. The school does not stand in for ethics, politics, or arithmetic.

exercises.prompt: What does this unit fix about a work, and what does it leave for later?

choices.text: It fixes the school by the volition premise, and leaves other standards of judgment for later
It fixes which prize the work must win

feedback.note: This unit identifies the school. Judging a work by the full standards of art is a further question, not this lesson.

exercises.prompt: Match each branch to what it covers, so the place of this school stays clear.

feedback.note: Romanticism is not a code of living and not a theory of force. It is a school inside the study of art.

exercises.prompt: Complete what the school projects.

parts.text: Romanticism projects man as able to

feedback.note: The projection is a being who can choose. Vanishing, mere obedience, and floating are not that projection.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence that states the projection.

feedback.note: That projection is the place of Romanticism in her esthetics: art that presents man as a being who chooses.
